source.title: Large language model scaling laws for neural quantum states in quantum chemistry
source.authors: Oliver Knitter; Dan Zhao; Stefan Leichenauer; Shravan K. Veerapaneni

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study adapts scaling-law analysis to neural quantum states and reports that the compute-optimal relationship varies by ansatz and loss metric, rather than following the approximately linear relationship it attributes to language models.
record.gate_note: The study's own fitted scaling curves and compute-constrained analyses are recorded below. Cited results about language-model scaling laws are not rows. Qualitative heat-map observations are not separately rowed because the text gives no separate numerical outcomes for them.
record.test_reason: It fits a Chinchilla-style power law (final loss vs parameters N and scaled training D') to its own 335 training runs of autoregressive neural quantum states (NQS) for quantum chemistry. It then derives compute-optimal allocations. This is a new, non-text regime (variational Monte Carlo, no training data), so its results bear on V5. They do not bear on the language-model-specific versions.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors fit Chinchilla-style curves to NQS absolute error and V-score using a problem-size-scaled training variable D'. They conclude the derived model-size/training-time relation is highly metric- and ansatz-dependent and does not match the approximately linear Chinchilla relation. They present the work as an initial ablation that invites a more comprehensive study.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a Chinchilla-style parametric curve and compute-constrained optimization, but adapts them to autoregressive NQS, absolute error and V-score, and D′=T×SF rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy and token count.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted coefficients and exponents, and derived compute-optimal allocation rates, differ by ansatz and by loss metric.

fits_no_version.finding: In NQS, the fitted exponents and the derived compute-optimal D'–N growth rate change strongly with ansatz and with the loss metric (V-score vs absolute error).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Outside language models, compute-optimal allocation from Chinchilla-style fits depends on architecture and evaluation metric.

record.problems: The study describes its dataset as an ablation and calls for a more comprehensive study with greater variety of architectures, problem sizes, and training setups. The reported log-R2 values range from 0.40 to 0.68. The compute-constrained analysis uses simplified FLOP estimates that the authors say trade accuracy for ease of computation.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numerical results relevant to the claim were left out. Qualitative heat-map descriptions in Figures 2, 4, and 5 were not added as rows because the text gives no separate numerical outcomes.

untested.parts: No extrapolation from small to much larger runs; no held-out-run prediction check.
No language-model compute-optimal allocation. The NQS allocation is derived from fits, not measured by IsoFLOP-style search.
Depth and width are not isolated at fixed N; hidden layers are kept fixed and shallow.
No language-model laws are compared. No alternative fitting methods, parameter counting rules or schedules are tested, and curvature away from a power law is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The setting is variational NQS with no training data; D' = steps × sampled fraction of search space stands in for tokens. Fits use final training loss, not held-out loss, and no uncertainty is reported. Model sizes are tiny (dimensions 8–128). The compute-optimal results are analytic consequences of the fits, not empirical optima, so they cannot confirm or refute V3. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study examines neural quantum states, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy of language models.
It does not report whether fits on small runs predict much larger runs.
The compute-constrained analysis concerns NQS, not language models; it does not test the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann comparison on language models.
It does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The tested setting is autoregressive NQS for quantum chemistry. Image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
It reports NQS ground-state metrics, not downstream language-model task performance.

The study shows dependence on ansatz and loss metric, but does not compare alternative parameter-counting rules, fitting methods, or training schedules to assess their effects on the fitted laws. It does not test curves bending away from a single power law across larger runs.

relationships.condition: Autoregressive NQS (MADE, RetNet, transformer) on seven small STO-3G molecules, final training V-score and absolute error
relationships.reason: The power-law form can be fitted, but log-R2 is only 0.40–0.68 (R1–R6). Some size exponents are extreme (α1 of 9.37 and 7.95), and the derived optimal D'–N exponents range from 0.38 to 8.28 depending on ansatz and metric (R7–R12).
relationships.display_finding: Fits reached log-R² values of 0.40–0.68, with size exponents as large as 9.37 and 7.95 and optimal D′–N exponents ranging from 0.38 to 8.28 across ansatz and metric choices.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope

reader_labels.reason: The derived compute-optimal allocation is a power relation in each setting, but its exponent varies substantially with ansatz and metric; the authors say the resulting rates do not reflect the approximately linear curves for language models (R7–R12).
